chapter_theme: The first twenty stanzas of Poigaiyar's Kalavazhi Narpathu: each paints one sight of the field where the Chola Sengan killed his enemies, elephants, blood, broken drums and scavengers, each in a single simile drawn mostly from hills, sea, rain and the farmer's tank, and each closes on the same refrain of the field where he killed.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem describes the field of the victor's killing

comparisons.tenor: the blood of the morning, dried by afternoon and kicked up

1.reading: On the field where the lord of the river country killed those who had wronged him, the blood of the fallen, deep enough to swallow swords, is churned by elephants until feet sink in it, lies as mud through the morning of the battle that met the rising sun, and by afternoon rises as dust red as coral.
1.nuance: The poem measures the slaughter by a single day: the same blood is mud in the forenoon and coral-coloured dust after noon, so the field's horror is shown through time rather than numbers. Line 3's முன்பசுல் is a misprint; the printed variant reads முற்பகல்.

thinai_evidence.note: the victor's battlefield is the subject

comparisons.tenor: blood flowing through the burst war drums under the dead elephants

2.reading: On the field where the lord of the river country roared and killed in battle, the bright blood that runs under the elephants lying dead on the ground and through the thundering drums whose skins have burst looks like water spouting from the sluices under the bund of a red tank after the monsoon rain.
2.nuance: The vehicle comes from the farmer's year, the full tank after the rains and its sluice, the same world that gives the genre its name of the threshing floor; the burst drum becomes the sluice pipe and the heaped elephants the bund.

thinai_evidence.note: the victor's field and the fighting in it

comparisons.tenor: the king's great drum, whose sound is a rain cloud's

3.reading: On the field where the lord of the water-rich land, whose great drum speaks like the rain cloud, killed those who erred against him, warriors who tire as they wade the streaming blood slip and rise again by leaning on the tusks of the fallen elephants.
3.nuance: The dead elephant becomes a staff for the living: the tusk that killed is now what a slipping soldier leans on to stand. The printed variant in line 2 reads எழூஉம் for எழுவர்.

thinai_evidence.note: the victor's field, named by its victor

comparisons.tenor: elephants carrying chariot wheels on their tusks

4.reading: On the field where Sengan killed those who would not yield, the elephants that smashed the handsome swift chariots and rose carrying those chariots' wheels on their tusks looked like mountains that the sun, moving across the wide sky, has come to rest upon.
4.nuance: The word for the wheel, பரிதி, is also a word for the sun, so the simile of the sun on the mountain is already latent in the noun; the poet only has to make the elephant a hill.

thinai_evidence.note: the victor's field, seen through its scavengers

comparisons.tenor: the blood-soaked crows

5.reading: On the field where Sengan killed those who had wronged him, the crows that plunged into and ate the blood of all the men opened by chosen arrows and spears lost their own colour, and now have the reddish back of the coucal and the red beak of the kingfisher.
5.nuance: The black crow is turned into two other birds by the blood it eats; the change of colour is the whole measure of the slaughter, and the poem never shows a body.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's victory over hostile kings

comparisons.vehicle: விசும்பி னுருமெறித் தெங்கும் பெருமலை தூறெறிந் தற்றே
comparisons.tenor: the elephants and corpses heaped across the field

6.reading: On the field where the Chola of the strong chariot, whose handsome chest bears ornaments of rare gems, killed the hostile kings, elephants lie piled across one another with corpses heaped in every direction, as if thunder had roared from the wide sky and struck down the thickets of great mountains everywhere.
6.nuance: The only verse of the chapter that names the victor by his line (செம்பியன், the Chola) and the defeated as kings (தெவ் வேந்தரை); the variant தூவெறிந்து in line 4 would make the thunder scatter rather than strike the thickets.

comparisons.tenor: the elephants before battle
the elephants after battle, covered in blood

7.reading: On the field where the lord of the Kaveri country, where red-eyed striped varal fish leap, killed his enemies, the elephants that looked like hills of collyrium before they churned the battle now appear like hills of vermilion.
7.nuance: Two similes, one before and one after, tell the battle as a change of colour from black to red without describing a blow; the red-eyed fish of the king's river repeat the red in his own peaceful country.

comparisons.tenor: elephants bristling with arrows

8.reading: On the field where the lord of the land of rushing water, with his thundering tuned drum, killed those who would not come near him, elephants crushed upon elephants, their bodies hidden by unceasing fierce arrows aimed at the eye, looked on every side like countless hills covered with flocks of sparrows.
8.nuance: The arrows standing out of the elephants' hides are the sparrows perched on a hill; the shafts, not the blood, carry the picture. The printed variant மெய்ம்மறைப்ப (line 2) makes the arrows cover the body rather than sink into it.

comparisons.tenor: severed anklet-wearing legs thrashing on the field

9.reading: On the field where the lord of the river country killed those who stood against him, the anklet-wearing legs of the men above, cut off with their leg-guards by the men below who came in close, toss about like hungry sharks in the dark sea.
9.nuance: மேலோர் and கீழோர் are most simply the riders on elephants and horses and the foot soldiers who cut at their legs from below; the words also carry rank, so the image is of the low cutting down the high. Line 3 is uncertain: சுற is a misprint for சுறா, and the variant reads நீலச் சுறா, blue sharks.

comparisons.tenor: arrow-pierced elephants standing still, red with blood

10.reading: On the field where the lord of the river country killed his foes, the elephants, pierced on every side by many arrows, cannot move and sink wearily where they stand, and look like hills of red earth of ancient renown.
10.nuance: The elephants do not fall: they stand, unable to go, and so become hills; the stillness that elsewhere is courage is here exhaustion (ஒல்கி உயங்கும்).

comparisons.tenor: the abandoned drums kicked by blinded elephants

11.reading: On the field where Sengan, unshaken in war, killed his enemies, the abandoned drums left behind by those whose strength failed in the thronging battle lie bathed in bright blood, and when the elephants, their work over and their eyes blinded, kick them, they boom like rain from dark clouds.
11.nuance: The drum, the voice of a king's army, still sounds after its army is gone, but now it is struck by blind feet; the opening word கழுமிய (thronging) may echo the name of the battlefield, Kazhumalam, though the verse does not name it. The variant மைந்திழந்தார் (line 1) says the same: those who lost their strength.

comparisons.tenor: elephants streaming blood from arrow wounds

12.reading: On the field where the lord of the Kaveri country drove on swiftly and killed those who would not join him, the handsome elephants, sagging as arrows pierce them without pause, with blood running from wounds like mouths of fire, look like beautiful hills of red earth, red at the summit, taking the downpour of a storm cloud.
12.nuance: Verse 10's red hill is here given rain: the blood running down the elephant is the storm water running down red earth, so the red of the hill is not only the elephant's colour but the colour the water carries.

comparisons.tenor: elephants
severed elephant trunks rolling on the ground

13.reading: On the field where the red warrior of battle strength fought and killed, the fighters thrust their long spears of ranked gleam and cut the trunks of the hill-like elephants, and the trunks roll like snakes struck by thunder on a mountain.
13.nuance: The two similes nest: the elephant is a hill, so its severed trunk is a snake that thunder has struck on that hill. செஎய் (line 4) is the king called by an epithet of red, or of Murugan; it is not a proper name.

thinai_evidence.note: the victor's field, with the defeated people named

comparisons.tenor: blood spurting from the cut trunks

14.reading: On the field where the lord of the river country killed the Kongar, the trunks of the elephants that take their balls of food, cut off, spurt bright red blood of glittering light like a bag spilling coral.
14.nuance: The only verse of the chapter to name the defeated: the Kongar, the people of the Kongu country. The trunk that a moment before was lifting food to the mouth now pours its own blood out like treasure from a bag.

comparisons.tenor: the field strewn with corpses and broken umbrellas

15.reading: On the field where the red-eyed, angry Sengan fought, wherever the killer elephants charged, smashing the royal umbrellas, corpses heaped up in every place they entered, so that the field looks like a carpenter's workshop.
15.nuance: The carpenter's shed is the most domestic image in the chapter: cut timbers and shavings everywhere, the work of a craftsman, so the killing is made to look like trade. Line 3 is garbled in the source (பள்ளிறிய் றோன்றும், read as பள்ளியிற் றோன்றும்).

comparisons.tenor: horses leaping onto the elephants' brows

16.reading: On the field where the lord of the river country killed the kings, the harnessed horses, urged on by picked warriors and undaunted by the roar of the shouting, leap onto the frontal globes of the elephants like great tigers springing up a hill.
16.nuance: ஆர்ப்பஞ்சா can belong to the horses (unafraid of the din) or to the elephants (unafraid of it, so the horses must climb them); either way the smaller animal, urged on (ஊக்கி), takes the larger like a tiger taking a hill.

comparisons.tenor: the bright drops of blood falling across the field

17.reading: On the field where the king roared and killed in battle, in the fight where shouting rose and man ran against man, striking and hurling, the bright blood that falls is like the many lamps of the Karthigai festival.
17.nuance: The festival of lamps, held in the dark month, gives the blood both its colour and its number: each falling drop a flame. The king is not named because the line that would name him is missing.

comparisons.tenor: corpses carried along in the flood of blood

18.reading: On the field where the king, whose garland buds are opening and whose sword leaves its sheath, killed those who had angered him, the blood drags the corpses of the dead along on every side like boats moving on the crowded sea.
18.nuance: The blood is now a sea and the dead its boats. Lines 3 and 4 are hard: தடற்றிடங்கொள் (variant தடற்றிலங்கொள்) and the editor's bracketed (ய்) in தார்ச்சே(ய்) leave the king's epithet uncertain.

comparisons.tenor: elephants with a spear-shaft standing out between their tusks

19.reading: On the field where the lord of the water country entered battle and killed, the spears hurled between the tusks sank in up to the shaft and left their butt-ends showing, so that the elephants, slowed in their gait, looked as if they had three tusks.
19.nuance: The wound makes the beast more fearsome-looking, a third tusk, at the very moment it weakens it (நடைமெலிந்து). கடைமணி is read here as the butt of the spear; the variant காழ் (shaft) for கால் supports this.

thinai_evidence.note: the victor's field, seen through its scavengers

comparisons.tenor: the vulture pulling at sinews of a corpse

20.reading: On the field where the lord of the river country killed those who stood against him, the vulture, spreading the quills of its ragged wings and tearing at the bloody corpses, looks like a musician tuning a fine drum that does not jar.
20.nuance: The vulture stretching and tugging at a corpse's sinews becomes a drummer tightening the thongs of his drum: the field after battle is turned into the rehearsal before a performance, as if the poet's own art were being prepared there.

links.note: Purananuru 369 (Paranar, thurai மறக்களவழி) builds the whole battle as a season of rain and tillage, elephants as clouds and arrows as rain on a wet field (ஈரச் செறுவயின்), ending in a request for elephants; Kalavazhi Narpathu 2 gives one farming image, blood running through burst drums like a tank's sluices after the monsoon (கார்ப்பெயல் பெய்தபின்).
links.teaches: Together they show how the kalavazhi theme changed form: Paranar's single sustained allegory of the farm year, made to earn a gift, becomes in Poigaiyar one quick water-and-field simile per stanza with no request, so the farming root of the genre's name survives only as a store of images.

links.note: Purananuru 19 (lines 8 to 9) likens arrows lodged in a wounded elephant to a flock of sparrows settled on a hill (குன்றத்து இறுத்த குரீஇஇனம் போல); Kalavazhi Narpathu 8 says elephants hidden by arrows look like countless hills with flocks of sparrows (எண்ணருங் குன்றிற் குரீஇயினம்).
links.teaches: The near-identical image shows a stock battle simile passing from a Pandya victory poem to a Chola one, and the frames show it carries no fixed feeling: in Purananuru 19 it leads into mothers weeping for sons and Death fleeing in shame, while in Poigaiyar it is pure spectacle of the victor's field.

links.note: Kural 597 holds up the elephant that plants its feet under a sheaf of arrows (புதையம்பிற் பட்டுப்பா டூன்றுங் களிறு) as the model of a mind that does not give way; Kalavazhi Narpathu 10 shows elephants pierced everywhere by arrows that cannot move and sink wearily where they stand (செல்கலா தொல்கி யுயங்கும்).
links.teaches: Seen from the battlefield, the Kural's emblem of steadfastness is ambiguous: the same arrow-struck elephant that stands its ground is, for the victor's poet, a beast too spent to move, so the maxim's courage depends on reading stillness as resolve rather than as defeat.

links.note: Purananuru 62 describes a battle in which both kings die, their drums are abandoned (முரசு ஒழிந்தனவே) and no one is left to claim the field (களங்கொளற்கு உரியோர் இன்றி); Kalavazhi Narpathu 11 describes the abandoned drums (ஒழிமுரசம்) of those whose strength failed, kicked by blinded elephants, on the field Sengan won.
links.teaches: The abandoned drum is the same sign in both, but whose drum it is decides what it means: when only the loser's drum is dropped it proves a victor and the field becomes his song, and when both drums fall, as in Purananuru 62, the field has no owner and the poet can only ask what the war was for.

links.note: Purananuru 373 (Kovur Kizhar, thurai மறக்களவழி) praises the Chola Killivalavan who made the Kongu turn their backs (கொங்கு புறம் பெற்ற) and ends among vultures on the fearful field, asking a gift; Kalavazhi Narpathu 14 names the Kongar as the enemy the lord of the river country killed (கொங்கரை அட்ட களத்து).
links.teaches: Read together they show that a Chola victory over the Kongu was already sung as a field-of-battle poem in the Purananuru, with the bard asking for his share; Poigaiyar keeps the enemy and the field but lets the stanza end on the field itself, turning a petition into a celebration complete without the bard's request.

links.note: Kural 599, in the chapter on energy (ஊக்கமுடைமை), says the elephant, for all its bulk and sharp tusks, fears a tiger's attack; Kalavazhi Narpathu 16 shows horses, urged on (ஊக்கி) by picked warriors, leaping onto the elephants' brows like tigers springing up a hill.
links.teaches: The battle verse turns the Kural's animal fable into tactics: the tiger's assault on the elephant is what cavalry does to war elephants, so the couplet's claim that drive overcomes size had a familiar picture on the field, and Poigaiyar's simile names the driving force with the Kural's own word.

source_issues: 1-20: the core record gives no thinai or thurai for any verse; all are marked vaakai here (Tholkappiyam places களவழி among the thurais of vaakai), and puram_thurai is empty.
1 line 3: முன்பசு லெல்லாம் is a misprint for முன்பகல் எல்லாம் (the variant reads முற்பகல்); the line is otherwise clear.
9 line 3: சுறபிறழ்வ is a misprint for சுறாப் பிறழ்வ; the printed variant runs the words together (இருங்கடலுணீலச்சுறாப்பிறழ்வ).
12 line 3: போன்றவெ for போன்றவே, as the misprint_candidate flag notes (tamilvu: போன்றனவே).
15 line 3: பள்ளிறிய் றோன்றும் is garbled; read as பள்ளியிற் றோன்றும்.
17: only four lines; tamilvu has five, and the missing line is most likely the one naming the king (its line 4 repeats verse 2's last line).
18 line 3: தார்ச்சே(ய்) carries the editor's bracketed letter; the variant தடற்றிலங்கொள்வாள் changes the sword phrase.
19 line 1: printed without word spaces (இடைமருப்பின்விட்டெறிந்தவெஃகங்கான் மூழ்திக்); மூழ்திக் is a misprint for மூழ்கிக், and the variant gives காழ் for கான்.
